title: What forgiveness isn't
hook: forgiving isn't excusing, forgetting, or staying in danger: Luke 17, Joseph, and David at the stronghold

segments.voice: Yesterday, Paul's list from a prison cell: whatsoever things are true, whatsoever things are lovely. Your line was guard your gaze. What did you give your hour off screens to? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-eight.

"Just forgive and forget." It gets said in kitchens, over the phone, sometimes to people who are still being hurt. It sounds biblical. It isn't. Those words aren't in the Bible. And when you read what the Bible does say about forgiving, it turns out to be harder than that slogan in one way, and much safer in another. So today, before saying what forgiveness is, a short list of what it isn't. It isn't excusing. It isn't forgetting. And it isn't staying in danger. Today: what forgiveness isn't.

First, it isn't excusing. Jesus says in Luke: "If thy brother trespass against thee, rebuke him; and if he repent, forgive him." The wrong gets named first. Excusing says it wasn't really wrong. Forgiving says it was, and then lets something go. What gets let go? The Greek word behind forgive here is aphiemi, and it means to let go, to release, to send away. It's what you do with a debt. You release the claim, the right to get even. You don't erase the record. Second, it isn't forgetting. At the end of Genesis, Joseph forgives the brothers who sold him into slavery, and he says it plainly: "ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good." He remembers exactly what they did. He forgives with the memory wide open. Third, and this one matters, it isn't staying in danger. In First Samuel, King Saul is hunting David to kill him. David has a chance to kill Saul in a cave, and spares him. Saul weeps and admits David is more righteous than he is. Then the story says Saul goes home, and David and his men go up to the stronghold. David doesn't move back into the palace. He leaves the judging to God, and he keeps his distance. Forgiveness and trust are different things. Trust may come back slowly, or not at all. If someone is hurting you, getting safe is not a failure to forgive.

Here's the practice: let go of the debt, keep the fence. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who hurt you. Not the deepest wound; something middle-sized. Name what they did, plainly, to yourself. Then notice the debt: the wish for them to pay, to hurt a little the way you did. See if you can set that down, even partway, while keeping whatever boundary keeps you safe. If this stirs up something heavy, stop, and talk with someone you trust. If you pray, you can use the line from the Lord's Prayer: "forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors." The bell holds the time.
What forgiveness isn't. Not calling a wrong right, not erasing the memory, not walking back into harm. It's letting go of the debt.

Your line: forgive and stay safe. Today, if you're carrying one old debt, see if you can release the getting even, while keeping the boundary that protects you. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-eight.

howItsDone: Christians pray "forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors" in the Lord's Prayer, and pastors and Christian counselors teach that forgiving a wrong does not require excusing it, forgetting it, or remaining in an unsafe relationship.

fork.setup: you're David. you've spared King Saul's life in a cave, and Saul has wept and called you more righteous than himself. now he's heading home. what do you do?
options: go home with him to the palace; it's all forgiven.
go up to the stronghold with your men.
follow him until he apologizes properly.
fork.reveal: Saul goes home, and David and his men go up to the stronghold. he spares his enemy and leaves the judging to God, but he doesn't walk back into danger either.

original.note: Greek: to let go, release, send away; a common New Testament word for forgiving a debt or a wrong.

trapdoor: what you thought: forgiving means acting like it never happened.
what it means: forgiving names the wrong, remembers it, and lets go of the right to get even, without walking back into danger.
what a scholar hears: aphiemi is the same verb used when the first disciples leave their nets (Matthew 4:20): to forgive is to let something go.
recall: the Latin word for this love

notes: Sensitive day: listeners may be in unsafe relationships. The script says getting safe is not a failure to forgive and invites anyone who is stirred up to talk with someone they trust; confirm tone, and whether a line pointing to local help should be added in the app around this day.

1 Samuel 24 paraphrased: David spares Saul in the cave (24:4–7); Saul weeps and says David is more righteous (24:16–17); Saul goes home and David and his men go up to the stronghold (24:22). Confirm the reading of 24:22 as keeping distance.
Greek aphiēmi glossed let go / release / send away; Matthew 4:20 'left their nets' uses a form of the same verb. Confirm.
'Those words aren't in the Bible' — the phrase 'forgive and forget' does not appear in the KJV; confirm.
Matthew 6:12 quoted as part of the Lord's Prayer (a real prayer), offered only as 'if you pray'.
The 'If he repent' condition in Luke 17:3 is quoted but not developed; churches differ on whether forgiveness waits for repentance. Consider a note for a future day.
